ἐναρχομένην. ἔοικε δὲ ἡ γραφὴ σφόδρα πολλαχοῦ διαφορὰν εἰδέναι θυμοῦ καὶ
ὀργῆς, ὥσπερ καὶ ἐν τῷ Κύριε μὴ τῷ θυμῷ ου ἐλέγξῃ με μηδὲ τῇ ὀργῇ ου παιδεύ ῃ
με. οὐχ ὁμοίως δὲ ὁριούμεθα τὸν ἐλέγχοντα θυμὸν Θεοῦ καὶ τὸν θυμὸν ὃν δεῖ
ἀρθῆναι ἀφ' ἡμῶν, οὐδὲ τὴν παιδεύου αν ὀργὴν Κυρίου καὶ τὴν ἡμετέραν. <τὰ μὲν
γὰρ περὶ Θεοῦ> τροπικώτερον εἴρηται, τὰ δὲ περὶ ἡμῶν ὀνομαζόμενα
ὁμολογουμένως πάθη ἐστὶ καὶ ἁμαρτήματα. κεῖται δὲ τὸ ὄνομα τῆς πικρίας καὶ ἐν τῷ
Ἱερεμίᾳ· καὶ ἡ πικρία γάρ ου, φησίν, ἀνέβη πρὸ μέ. οἶμαι οὖν πικρίαν μὲν νῦν
λέγεσθαι παρὰ τῷ ἀποστόλῳ καθὸ λέγομεν τινὰς πικροὺς ἐναντίους τοῖς γλυκέσι,
καὶ ἡ συνήθεια γὰρ γλυκεῖς ἀνθρώπους οἶδε καὶ πικρούς· θυμὸν δὲ τὴν ἐναρχομένην
ἐπί τινι γενέσθαι ὀργὴν ἐν τῇ ψυχῇ· ὀργὴν δὲ τάχα οὐ τὸ γένος τούτων καὶ ἑτέρων
παραπλησίων, ἀλλὰ τὴν ἤδη ἑτοίμην καὶ ἐνεργητικὴν πρὸς τὴν «τιμωρίαν τοῦ
ἠδικηκέναι νομιζομένου.» καὶ ὡς ἐπίπαν παρακολουθεῖ τοῖς πάθεσι τούτοις καὶ ἡ
κραυγή, κεκραγότων τῶν πικραινομένων καὶ θυμουμένων καὶ ὀργιζομένων, καὶ
θορυβωδέστερον λαλούν των καὶ προφερομένων λόγους καὶ πικρίας καὶ θυμοῦ καὶ
ὀργῆς. διὸ πρὸς τοῖς προτέροις καὶ κραυγὴν ἀσκητέον ἀρθῆναι ἀφ' ἡμῶν. οἶμαι δὲ
ἐνθάδε βλασφημίαν ἣν κελεύει ἀρθῆναι ἀφ' ἡμῶν ἣν προφέρονται ἀπὸ παθῶν
ὀργιζόμενοι πολλάκις οἱ καὶ κατὰ τοῦ θείου τολμῶντες ἐν τῷ καιρῷ τῆς ὀργῆς
λαλεῖν, ὅταν πᾶσα ἡ κατηγορία περὶ οὑτινοσοῦν λαμβάνηται αὖθις ἐν τῇ βλασφημίᾳ·
βλασφημεῖν γὰρ λέγονται οἱ κακῶς λέγοντες ἐκείνους οὓς λέγουσι κακῶς. διὸ
ἀκολούθως τοῖς περὶ πικρίας καὶ θυμοῦ καὶ ὀργῆς καὶ κραυγῆς λέγεται δεῖν
ἀποτίθεσθαι καὶ τὴν βλασφημίαν. εἰ μέντοιγε καὶ τὴν βλασφημίαν τάσσοιμεν ἐπὶ
πάσης φωνῆς τῆς κακῶς τὸ θεῖον λεγούσης, οὐ μόνον ἐκ λύπης καὶ ὀργῆς κατὰ τοὺς
καιροὺς τῆς δυσαρεστή σεως δυσφημούντων τῶν ἀνθρώπων ἀλλὰ πολλάκις καὶ
κατὰ ἄγνοιαν τοῦ περὶ ἀληθείας λόγου, ὡς δῆλον ἐκ τῶν παρὰ τοῖς ἑτεροδόξοις
δογμάτων, βλασφημεῖ δὴ καὶ ὁ τὸν ἀληθῆ λόγον ψευδῆ ἀποφαινόμενος εἶναι ἢ τὸν
ψευδῆ ἀληθῆ, καὶ μάλιστα περὶ Θεοῦ καὶ τῶν τοῦ Θεοῦ πραγμάτων. τίς οὖν οὕτως
δόκιμο τραπεζίτη ὡς εἰδέναι πάντα δοκιμάζειν καὶ τὸ μὲν καλὸν κατέχειν ἀπὸ δὲ
παντὸ εἴδου πονηροῦ ἀπέχε θαι; ἐπεὶ δέ τινες οἴονται εὐλόγως ποτὲ γίνεσθαι ὀργήν,
μὴ καλῶς προστιθέντες τῷ εὐαγγελίῳ τὸ «εἰκῇ» κατὰ τὸ ῥητόν ὃ ἂν ὀργιθῇ τῷ
ἀδελφῷ αὐτοῦ ἔνοχο ἔ ται τῇ κρί ειἀνέγνωσαν γάρ τινες ὃ ἐὰν ὀργι θῇ τῷ ἀδελφῷ
αὐτοῦ εἰκῇ– δυσωπήσωμεν αὐτοὺς ἐκ τοῦ προκειμένου ῥητοῦ λέγοντος πᾶσα πικρία
καὶ θυμὸς καὶ ὀργὴ καὶ κραυγὴ καὶ βλασφημία ἀρθήτω ἀφ' ὑμῶν. σαφῶς γὰρ ἐνθάδε
ἡ πᾶσα φωνὴ κατὰ κοινοῦ ἐπὶ πάντων εἴρηται, ὡς μηδεμιᾶς πικρίας συγχωρουμένης
μηδὲ θυμοῦ τινος ἐπιτρεπομένου μηδὲ ὀργῆς τινος εὐλόγως συνερχομένης. καὶ ἐν
τριακοστῷ ἕκτῳ ψαλμῷ, ὡς πάσης ὀργῆς ἁμαρτίας οὔσης (ὁμοίως δὲ καὶ θυμοῦ),
λέγεται παῦ αι ἀπὸ ὀργῆ καὶ ἐγκατάλειπε θυμόν. οὐκοῦν οὐκ ἔστιν ποτὲ εὐλόγως
ὀργισθῆναί τινι. καὶ οὐ μόνον γε πᾶσαν πικρίαν καὶ πάντα θυμὸν καὶ πᾶσαν ὀργὴν
καὶ πᾶσαν βλασφημίαν φιλοπονητέον ἀρθῆναι ἀφ' ἡμῶν, ἀλλὰ ταῦτα σὺν πάσῃ
κακίᾳ· κακίαν δὲ ἐκλαμβάνομεν ἤτοι τὴν ἐναντίαν ἕξιν τῇ ἀρετῇ ἢ τὴν πονηρίαν. 23

And scripture seems very often in many places to know a difference of wrath and anger, as also in: Lord, do not in your wrath rebuke me nor in your anger discipline me. But we will not define alike the rebuking wrath of God and the wrath which must be taken away from us, nor the disciplining anger of the Lord and ours. For the things about God are said more figuratively, but the things named about us are admittedly passions and sins. And the name of bitterness lies also in Jeremiah: and your bitterness, he says, went up to me. I think therefore bitterness is now said by the apostle in the way we call some bitter, contrary to the sweet ones, for usage also knows sweet people and bitter. And wrath the anger beginning to come to be at something in the soul; and anger perhaps not the genus of these and of other similar ones, but the one already ready and active toward the punishment of the one thought to have done wrong. And as a whole clamor also follows these passions, those becoming bitter and wrathful and angry crying out, and speaking more tumultuously and bringing forward words of bitterness and wrath and anger. Wherefore besides the former ones one must practice also clamor being taken away from us. And I think the blasphemy here which he orders to be taken from us is that which those angry often bring forward from passions, those who also dare against the divine to speak in the time of anger, when every accusation about anyone whatever is taken again in the blasphemy; for those speaking badly of those they speak badly of are said to blaspheme. Wherefore consequently to the things about bitterness and wrath and anger and clamor it is said that one must put off also blasphemy. If however we should rank blasphemy also upon every voice speaking badly of the divine, not only of men speaking ill from grief and anger in the times of displeasure but often also according to ignorance of the account about truth, as is clear from the doctrines among the other-opinioned, he also blasphemes who declares the true account to be false or the false true, and most of all about God and the matters of God. Who then is so approved a banker as to know to test all things and to hold the good and to keep away from every form of evil? But since some think anger sometimes comes to be reasonably, not well adding to the gospel the without cause according to the saying: whoever is angry with his brother will be liable to the judgment (for some read: whoever is angry with his brother without cause), let us shame them from the present saying, saying: let all bitterness and wrath and anger and clamor and blasphemy be taken from you. For clearly here the all word is said in common upon all, so that no bitterness is conceded nor any wrath permitted nor any anger coming together reasonably. And in the thirty-sixth psalm, as all anger being sin (and likewise also wrath), it is said: cease from anger and abandon wrath. Therefore it is not possible ever reasonably to be angry with someone. And not only all bitterness and all wrath and all anger and all blasphemy must one labor to be taken from us, but these with all malice; and malice we take either the contrary habit to virtue or wickedness. [4:32] Become to one another kind, compassionate, forgiving yourselves as also God in Christ forgave us. Origen says: we named the contrary to the bitter sweet; but Paul seems now to call the contrary order to bitterness kindness, metaphorically from the foods; thus therefore we can understand the become kind to one another instead of: some approachable and in character sweet and gentle. And this happens if, having put off the raw and merciless and unsympathetic toward the neighbor, we become compassionate toward all, through these granting the greatest things not only to the ones near but also to ourselves; forgiving yourselves being other than forgiving one another, since whatever we do well to others in benefiting, these things, both because of the end and because of our being of one body, are referred more to us than to those we think we have done well to. And these things we grant to ourselves, as many as God also granted us in Christ, as it were receiving them and keeping and imitating the one who granted and his manner of granting. Scripture seems in very many places to know a difference between wrath and anger, as in “Lord, do not rebuke me in your wrath, nor discipline me in your anger.” Yet we will not define in the same way the wrath of God that rebukes and the wrath that must be put away from us, nor the anger of the Lord that disciplines and our own. For what is said of God is said more figuratively, while what is named in us is, by common consent, passions and sins.

The word bitterness occurs also in Jeremiah: “And your bitterness,” he says, “has come up to me.” So I think the apostle is now speaking of bitterness in the sense in which we call some people bitter, the opposite of sweet; for common usage knows both sweet people and bitter ones. Wrath is the anger that is beginning to arise in the soul at something; and anger, perhaps, is not the genus of these and of others like them, but anger already ready and active for “the punishment of one thought to have done wrong.” And clamor, as a rule, follows these passions too: the bitter, the wrathful and the angry shout, and speak more noisily, and bring out words of bitterness, wrath and anger. So, in addition to the former, we must also train ourselves to have clamor put away from us.

The blasphemy here, which he commands to be put away from us, is, I think, what people often bring out from passion when they are angry, people who in the moment of anger dare to speak even against the divine; and blasphemy is again taken to cover every accusation against anyone at all, since those who speak ill of others are said to blaspheme those they speak ill of. So, following the words about bitterness and wrath and anger and clamor, it is said that blasphemy too must be put away.

If, however, we were also to class as blasphemy every utterance that speaks ill of the divine, not only when people speak evil out of grief and anger in times of displeasure, but often also from ignorance of the teaching of the truth, as is clear from the doctrines held among the heterodox, then the one who declares the true teaching false, or the false true, blasphemes too, above all about God and the things of God. Who, then, is so approved a money-changer as to know how to test everything, to hold fast to what is good and to keep away from every form of evil (1 Thessalonians 5:21–22)?

Some think that anger sometimes arises with good reason. They wrongly add to the gospel the words “without cause” in the saying “Whoever is angry with his brother will be liable to judgment” (Matthew 5:22); for some have read “whoever is angry with his brother without cause.” Let us put them to shame with the present text, which says, “Let all bitterness and wrath and anger and clamor and blasphemy be put away from you.” For here the word “all” is plainly said in common of them all, so that no bitterness is allowed, no wrath is permitted, and no anger comes upon us with good reason. And in Psalm 37, as though all anger were sin (and wrath likewise), it is said, “Cease from anger and forsake wrath” (Psalm 37:8). So it is never reasonable to be angry with anyone. And we must work hard to have put away from us not only all bitterness and all wrath and all anger and all blasphemy, but these together with all malice; and by malice we understand either the state opposed to virtue, or wickedness.

“Be kind to one another, tenderhearted, forgiving yourselves, as God in Christ also forgave us” (Ephesians 4:32). Origen says: we named sweet as the opposite of bitter; but Paul seems now to call kindness what stands opposite bitterness, by a metaphor taken from foods. So we can understand “Be kind to one another” as meaning “people easy to approach, sweet and gentle in character.” This happens if we put away harshness, mercilessness and want of sympathy toward our neighbor and become tenderhearted toward all; and by this we give the greatest gifts not only to those near us but also to ourselves. For “forgiving yourselves” is something other than “forgiving one another,” since whatever good we do to others when we benefit them returns to ourselves, both because of its end and because we are of one body, more than to those we seem to have helped. And we give ourselves all that God also gave us in Christ, as it were receiving these gifts, keeping them, and imitating the Giver and his way of giving. choices.term: διὰ τὸ συσσώμους ἡμᾶς εἶναι (OCR “υ ώμου”)
choices.english: because we are of one body
choices.why: The OCR reads “υ ώμου”; σ dropped twice gives συσσώμους (Ephesians 3:6). The old English “by our being under the law” has no support in the Greek.
χαρίζομαι means both “forgive” and “grant as a gift”; Origen plays on both, so the lemma keeps “forgiving” and his comment uses “give”.
Kept apart throughout, because Origen’s argument rests on the difference.
